> **A:** **Q:** What is the skill-disposition gap in critical thinking?
> **A:** A person can possess CT skills (ability to analyze, evaluate, infer) but fail to deploy them — defaulting to System 1 responses, motivated reasoning, or intellectual passivity. Dispositions (truth-seeking, open-mindedness, intellectual courage) determine whether skills are actually activated. Research shows modest correlations between skill and disposition measures, demonstrating partial independence.
> **Recall cue:** Skills = ability; Dispositions = tendency; Gap = having without using

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[critical-thinking-foundational-report-2026-04-01]])*
> **Q:** SR-13: Definition — Confirmation Bias
> **A:** **Q:** What are the three forms of confirmation bias?
> **A:** (1) Biased information search — seeking evidence that confirms existing beliefs. (2) Biased interpretation — interpreting ambiguous evidence as supporting prior views. (3) Biased memory — selectively recalling confirming information. Operates automatically, often below conscious awareness, making metacognitive monitoring essential for detection.
> **Recall cue:** Search / Interpret / Remember — all biased toward confirmation

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Q:** What is the difference between a textbase and a situation model in reading comprehension?
> **A:** **A:** A *textbase* is a propositional semantic representation of what the text explicitly says — a network of propositions derived from the text's surface content. A *situation model* is a richer mental model of the actual situation, event, or concept described by the text, incorporating prior knowledge, inferences, spatial relationships, and causal structure. Situation models support transfer and problem-solving; textbase representations support paraphrase and recognition.
> **Difficulty:** Basic | **Tags:** #reading-comprehension #cognitive-science

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Q:** What is the Fluency Illusion, and why does it undermine metacognitive monitoring?
> **A:** **A:** The Fluency Illusion is the systematic tendency to interpret *ease of text processing* (perceptual fluency) as evidence of *comprehension depth*, when fluency and comprehension are not reliably related. Re-reading increases fluency without necessarily improving situation model quality — but the increased fluency feels like improved understanding. This creates false metacognitive confidence and is a primary driver of the passive re-reading trap.
> **Source:** Section 8.2 | **Difficulty:** Intermediate | **Tags:** #metacognition #fluency-illusion

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Q:** What are the three sub-types of metacognitive knowledge, and which is most predictive of strategic reading proficiency?
> **A:** **A:** (1) *Declarative* — knowing *what* strategies exist; (2) *Procedural* — knowing *how* to execute strategies; (3) *Conditional* — knowing *when* and *why* to use which strategy. Conditional metacognitive knowledge is most predictive of advanced reading proficiency and hardest to develop through instruction.
> **Source:** Section 3.1 | **Difficulty:** Intermediate | **Tags:** #metacognition #self-regulated-learning

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Q:** What is the Matthew Effect in reading, and what does this report claim about its interaction with metacognitive monitoring?
> **A:** **A:** The Matthew Effect describes how early reading advantages (vocabulary, comprehension) compound over time — rich get richer, poor get poorer in literacy development. This report's synthesis argues that the Matthew Effect creates a *double failure trap*: poor domain knowledge simultaneously degrades comprehension (less effective schema application) and degrades metacognitive monitoring accuracy (schemas needed for monitoring failures are absent). Both deficits compound each other.
> **Source:** Section 6.4 | **Difficulty:** Advanced | **Tags:** #matthew-effect #metacognition #prior-knowledge

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Q:** According to Dunlosky et al. (2013), which learning strategies have high utility? Which have low utility?
> **A:** **A:** **High utility:** retrieval practice (practice testing) and spaced repetition. **Moderate utility:** elaborative interrogation, self-explanation, interleaving. **Low utility:** re-reading and highlighting. The high-utility strategies are underused by most students despite being most effective; the low-utility strategies are overused because they feel effective (due to Fluency Illusion).
> **Source:** Section 5.2 | **Difficulty:** Basic | **Tags:** #learning-strategies #retrieval-practice

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Q:** What is Reciprocal Teaching, and what four strategies does it involve?
> **A:** **A:** Reciprocal Teaching (Palincsar & Brown, 1984) is a scaffolded reading comprehension intervention involving small groups rotating through four metacognitive strategies: (1) **Summarizing** — capturing main points to check integration; (2) **Question generating** — formulating key questions to promote elaboration; (3) **Clarifying** — addressing confusing terms or passages; (4) **Predicting** — using text structure to anticipate upcoming content. Each strategy constitutes a component of the metacognitive monitoring-and-control cycle.
> **Source:** Section 7.2 | **Difficulty:** Basic | **Tags:** #reciprocal-teaching #reading-instruction #metacognition

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Q:** What is the Zone of Proximal Development, and how does it apply to reading comprehension instruction?
> **A:** **A:** Vygotsky's ZPD defines the range of tasks a learner cannot manage independently but can manage with appropriate support. In reading instruction, the ZPD identifies texts and tasks where comprehension is possible with scaffolding but would fail without it. Optimal instruction targets the ZPD — neither too easy (no challenge) nor too difficult (incomprehensible even with support). Scaffolding is gradually reduced as the learner's independent competence develops (I-We-You progression).
> **Difficulty:** Basic | **Tags:** #vygotsky #scaffolding #zone-of-proximal-development

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Q:** What is conditional metacognitive knowledge, and why is it more powerful than declarative or procedural metacognitive knowledge for reading?
> **A:** **A:** Conditional metacognitive knowledge is knowing *when* and *why* to apply specific reading strategies — understanding the match between strategy type, text type, and comprehension goal. It is more powerful than declarative knowledge (knowing strategies exist) or procedural knowledge (knowing how to execute them) because it enables strategic flexibility: deploying the right strategy in the right context rather than applying favorite strategies indiscriminately. This strategy-selection capacity is the metacognitive master skill.
> **Difficulty:** Advanced | **Tags:** #metacognitive-knowledge #conditional-knowledge #strategy-selection

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Q:** What is elaborative interrogation, and what mechanism explains its effectiveness?
> **A:** **A:** Elaborative interrogation is a reading strategy involving self-generated "Why is this true?" questions after encountering factual or explanatory claims. Its effectiveness is explained by multiple converging mechanisms: (1) prior knowledge activation (retrieving related schemas); (2) semantic elaboration (connecting the claim to a knowledge network, creating multiple retrieval pathways); (3) inference generation (producing causal inferences beyond text information); (4) comprehension monitoring (inability to generate a plausible "why" signals comprehension failure).
> **Source:** Section 5.2 | **Difficulty:** Intermediate | **Tags:** #elaborative-interrogation #deep-processing

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Q:** What is the Nelson-Narens monitoring-control model, and what is the key distinction it draws?
> **A:** **A:** The Nelson-Narens (1990) model describes metacognitive functioning as a two-level system: the *object level* (the actual cognitive reading processes — word recognition, sentence parsing, situation model construction) and the *meta level* (the monitoring and control system operating on object-level processes). *Monitoring* = information flow from object to meta level (the meta system's observation of comprehension state). *Control* = information flow from meta to object level (executive regulation of reading behavior in response to monitoring). Key insight: monitoring and control are distinct — readers can monitor failures without deploying appropriate control responses.
> **Source:** Section 3.2 | **Difficulty:** Advanced | **Tags:** #metacognition #nelson-narens #monitoring-control

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[goal-setting-and-assessment-in-pkm-foundational-report-2026-04-15]])*
> **Q:** SR Seed 1 — Definition
> **A:** **Q:** What are the four mechanisms through which goals affect performance according to Locke and Latham's Goal-Setting Theory?
> **A:** Goals (1) direct attention towards goal-relevant activities, (2) energise effort proportional to goal difficulty, (3) promote persistence, and (4) stimulate the discovery and use of task-relevant strategies.
> **Source:** Section 1 | **Difficulty:** Basic | **Tags:** #goal-setting-theory #locke-latham

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[goal-setting-and-assessment-in-pkm-foundational-report-2026-04-15]])*
> **Q:** SR Seed 2 — Distinction
> **A:** **Q:** What is the key distinction between mastery-approach and performance-approach goals in Elliot's 2×2 Achievement Goal framework?
> **A:** Mastery-approach goals are oriented toward developing competence (learning, improving); performance-approach goals are oriented toward demonstrating competence relative to others (outperforming, proving ability). Both have approach valence, but mastery goals are associated with deeper processing and intrinsic interest while performance goals are associated with surface strategies.
> **Source:** Section 1 | **Difficulty:** Intermediate | **Tags:** #achievement-goal-theory #elliot

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[goal-setting-and-assessment-in-pkm-foundational-report-2026-04-15]])*
> **Q:** SR Seed 3 — Definition
> **A:** **Q:** What are the three basic psychological needs identified by Self-Determination Theory, and why do they matter for PKM?
> **A:** Autonomy (experiencing choice and volitional engagement), competence (feeling effective and capable), and relatedness (feeling connected to others). In PKM, satisfaction of these needs is associated with autonomous motivation — which predicts deeper learning, greater persistence, more creative processing, and higher well-being than controlled motivation.
> **Source:** Section 2 | **Difficulty:** Basic | **Tags:** #sdt #basic-psychological-needs

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[goal-setting-and-assessment-in-pkm-foundational-report-2026-04-15]])*
> **Q:** SR Seed 4 — Process
> **A:** **Q:** What are the three phases of Zimmerman's cyclical model of self-regulated learning?
> **A:** (1) Forethought — goal-setting, strategic planning, self-efficacy beliefs; (2) Performance — self-monitoring, strategy implementation, attention focusing; (3) Self-reflection — self-evaluation, causal attribution, adaptive revision. These phases cycle continually rather than following a one-time linear sequence.
> **Source:** Section 3 | **Difficulty:** Basic | **Tags:** #srl #zimmerman

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[goal-setting-and-assessment-in-pkm-foundational-report-2026-04-15]])*
> **Q:** SR Seed 5 — Connection
> **A:** **Q:** How does the GRM Triad differ from a linear model of goal → regulation → metacognition?
> **A:** The GRM Triad treats goal formulation, self-regulation, and metacognitive monitoring as three simultaneously active vertices of a dynamic system, each capable of initiating change in the others, rather than as sequential stages. This means metacognitive monitoring can revise goals directly (not just evaluate performance), and goal changes can alter the character of monitoring (not just provide targets).
> **Source:** Section 4 | **Difficulty:** Advanced | **Tags:** #grm-triad #original-contribution

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[goal-setting-and-assessment-in-pkm-foundational-report-2026-04-15]])*
> **Q:** SR Seed 6 — Distinction
> **A:** **Q:** What is the difference between informational and controlling assessment, and why does it matter for PKM?
> **A:** Informational assessment provides data about learning state (here's what you know, here's where gaps remain) and supports autonomy. Controlling assessment evaluates the person's worth (you're doing well/poorly) and creates pressure to perform. Informational assessment sustains intrinsic motivation; controlling assessment undermines it. PKB review protocols should generate informational, not controlling, feedback.
> **Source:** Section 5 | **Difficulty:** Intermediate | **Tags:** #assessment #sdt #feedback

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[goal-setting-and-assessment-in-pkm-foundational-report-2026-04-15]])*
> **Q:** SR Seed 7 — Application
> **A:** **Q:** Name the five layers of the PKB Goal Scaffolding Architecture and the temporal scale at which each operates.
> **A:** (1) Direction Layer — long-term, quarterly review; (2) Project Layer — bounded periods, monthly review; (3) Cycle Layer — fortnightly, implements forethought; (4) Session Layer — single sessions, implements performance + reflection; (5) Assessment Layer — multi-scale (micro/meso/macro), provides informational feedback.
> **Source:** Section 6 | **Difficulty:** Intermediate | **Tags:** #pkb-architecture #original-contribution

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[goal-setting-and-assessment-in-pkm-foundational-report-2026-04-15]])*
> **Q:** SR Seed 8 — Connection
> **A:** **Q:** What are the three developmental stages of self-regulatory capacity in PKM, and what characterises each?
> **A:** (1) Other-regulated — relies on external scaffolding (templates, prescribed protocols, community guidance), goals often adopted from external sources. (2) Co-regulated — internalising regulatory processes while benefiting from external support; increasing self-generation of goals. (3) Self-regulated — internalised GRM Triad processes operating fluently; PKB as extended mind rather than external support. Even self-regulated learners revert to other-regulation in new domains.
> **Source:** Section 7 | **Difficulty:** Intermediate | **Tags:** #developmental-trajectory #self-regulation

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[goal-setting-and-assessment-in-pkm-foundational-report-2026-04-15]])*
> **Q:** SR Seed 9 — Distinction
> **A:** **Q:** What is metacognitive calibration, and why is it a central concern for PKM practice?
> **A:** Metacognitive calibration is the accuracy of monitoring judgements relative to actual performance — the degree to which what you think you know matches what you actually know. Poor calibration (overconfidence or underconfidence) leads to misallocated study effort, premature closure on partially understood topics, or unnecessary review of mastered material. Calibration is learnable and improves with domain experience and deliberate self-testing.
> **Source:** Section 4 | **Difficulty:** Advanced | **Tags:** #metacognition #calibration

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[goal-setting-and-self-regulated-learning-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Q:** Definition | Intention-Action Gap
> **A:** **Front**: What is the "intention-action gap" and what does Sheeran's meta-analysis reveal about the strength of intentions as predictors of behavior?
> **Back**: The intention-action gap is the systematic failure of sincerely formed intentions to generate corresponding action. Sheeran's meta-analysis found that intentions account for only ~28% of behavioral variance — a modest relationship, with the gap most severe for novel, complex behaviors requiring sustained effort. The gap is primarily architectural (absence of specific volitional structures) rather than motivational.

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[goal-setting-and-self-regulated-learning-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Q:** Distinction | Goal Specificity vs. Goal Commitment
> **A:** **Front**: Distinguish goal specificity from goal commitment. Which is a necessary condition for the feedback loop, and which is the primary moderator of the difficulty-performance relationship?
> **Back**: **Goal specificity** is the precision of the performance standard — necessary for the feedback-standard comparison loop that drives regulatory adjustment. **Goal commitment** is the determination to pursue the goal despite obstacles — the primary moderator of the difficulty-performance relationship. Both are required: specificity without commitment produces clear targets without follow-through; commitment to a vague goal cannot close the monitoring loop.

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[goal-setting-and-self-regulated-learning-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Q:** Process | Zimmerman's SRL Phases
> **A:** **Front**: Describe the three phases of Zimmerman's Cyclical SRL Model and identify the single most consequential process in each phase for long-term learning development.
> **Back**: (1) **Forethought**: Goal-setting and strategic planning most consequential — determines the quality of goal architecture feeding all downstream monitoring. (2) **Performance**: Self-observation/monitoring most consequential — generates the feedback against which performance can be evaluated. (3) **Self-Reflection**: Causal attribution most consequential — determines whether performance information generates adaptive or maladaptive inferences for the next cycle, making the model genuinely recursive or merely repetitive.

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[goal-setting-and-self-regulated-learning-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Q:** Definition | Implementation Intention
> **A:** **Front**: What is an implementation intention? What is its mechanism, and what does it accomplish that goal intentions alone cannot?
> **Back**: An implementation intention is an "if-then" plan: "If [situational cue], then [goal-directed response]." Mechanism: creates a prospective memory link that automatizes cue-initiated behavior, bypassing voluntary recall. What it accomplishes: reduces volitional demand at initiation by converting a deliberate decision into an automatic cue-triggered response. This addresses the prospective memory failure problem — the failure to *remember* to act when the opportunity arises — while leaving goal commitment unchanged.

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[goal-setting-and-self-regulated-learning-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Q:** Application | Action Orientation vs. State Orientation
> **A:** **Front**: What is Kuhl's distinction between action orientation and state orientation, and what is the regulatory consequence of each under conditions of difficulty and failure?
> **Back**: **Action orientation**: attention directed toward task-relevant problem-solving strategies; cognitive resources remain goal-directed under difficulty. **State orientation**: attention directed toward internal emotional states (rumination, anxiety); cognitive resources consumed by affective processing rather than problem-solving. Under failure: action-oriented learners process negative affect and return to goal-directed cognition; state-oriented learners remain in affective preoccupation, functionally blocking continued goal-directed behavior.

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[goal-setting-and-self-regulated-learning-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Q:** Distinction | Mastery vs. Performance Goal Orientation (Adaptive Regulation)
> **A:** **Front**: How do mastery and performance goal orientations produce different regulatory responses to failure, and why?
> **Back**: **Mastery**: failure interpreted as strategic information — signals which approach is not working, activates strategy search and effort intensification. Failure is informative rather than identity-threatening, so regulatory response is approach rather than avoidance. **Performance**: failure interpreted as evidence of lower ability or standing relative to others — activates defensive processing, self-protective withdrawal, and disengagement. Because performance goals define success comparatively, failure carries identity-threatening content that mastery-framed failure does not.

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[goal-setting-and-self-regulated-learning-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Q:** Definition | Metacognitive Calibration
> **A:** **Front**: What is metacognitive calibration and why is it important for SRL? What is the core limitation of endogenous calibration in novice learners?
> **Back**: Metacognitive calibration is the accuracy of the correspondence between self-assessed understanding and actual understanding. Crucial for SRL because inaccurate monitoring generates maladaptive regulatory decisions — specifically, prematurely moving on from inadequately processed material. Core limitation: novices lack the domain standards needed to evaluate their own knowledge quality (Dunning-Kruger), creating systematically overconfident monitoring. Solution: externally-sourced calibration (retrieval practice, error analysis, expert feedback) provides accurate performance signals the endogenous system cannot.

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[goal-setting-and-self-regulated-learning-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Q:** Connection | SDT and Achievement Goal Theory
> **A:** **Front**: What is the relationship between Self-Determination Theory's autonomous/controlled distinction and Achievement Goal Theory's mastery/performance distinction? Are they independent?
> **Back**: Partially overlapping but distinguishable. Mastery-approach goals are more likely to be autonomously regulated; performance-avoidance goals more likely controlled. However, the dimensions are not identical: a performance-approach goal can be autonomously adopted (genuinely desiring to achieve high comparative standing) and a mastery goal can be controlled (experiencing mastery pursuit as obligatory). SDT's distinction concerns the *source* of motivation (autonomous vs. controlled); achievement goal theory concerns the *definition of success* (competence development vs. comparative standing). Both independently predict engagement quality and outcomes.

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[goal-setting-and-self-regulated-learning-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Q:** Process | The Self-Concordance Mechanism
> **A:** **Front**: What is the self-concordance model, what does it predict, and what is the mechanism that explains why self-concordant goals produce better long-term outcomes?
> **Back**: Self-concordance (Sheldon & Elliot): degree to which pursued goals align with genuine personal values rather than external pressure. Predicts greater sustained effort, better obstacle-weathering, higher attainment probability, and greater wellbeing upon attainment. Mechanism: self-concordant goal pursuit satisfies basic psychological needs (competence, autonomy, relatedness), which sustain intrinsic motivation and continued investment. Non-self-concordant goals, even when attained, fail to generate need satisfaction because the pursuit was not genuinely one's own — producing the "arrival fallacy" of hollow achievement.

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[goal-setting-and-self-regulated-learning-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Q:** Definition | Volitional Control
> **A:** **Front**: What is volitional control and why does it function as the "neglected middle" of learning psychology?
> **Back**: Volitional control: the capacity to translate committed intentions into sustained action, protecting goal pursuit against competing motivations, environmental distractions, emotional disturbances, and cognitive temptations. "Neglected middle": it occupies the space between motivation (studied extensively in the predecisional phase) and metacognition (studied during task execution), but the specific mechanisms by which commitment is sustained *across* learning episodes were historically under-theorized. Volition is distinct from motivation (which initiates) and metacognition (which monitors); it is the sustaining capacity that maintains goal-directed behavior when motivation fluctuates.

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[goal-setting-and-self-regulated-learning-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Q:** Application | Building a Goal Architecture
> **A:** **Front**: List the five components of an effective goal architecture based on the integrated framework in this report.
> **Back**: 1. **Decomposition**: Long-horizon aspirations broken into specific proximal milestones with clear success criteria; 2. **Challenge calibration**: Goals set at the upper edge of credible attainability (productive struggle range); 3. **Feedback structure**: Explicit mechanisms for generating real-time performance-to-standard comparison data; 4. **Implementation intentions**: "If-then" behavioral plans for each significant learning activity; 5. **Motivational check**: Self-concordance verification — explicit connection to genuine personal values rather than external compliance.

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[goal-setting-and-self-regulated-learning-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Q:** Connection | Goal-Setting Theory Mechanisms → SRL Phase Mapping
> **A:** **Front**: Map Locke and Latham's four mediating mechanisms (direction, effort, persistence, strategy activation) onto Zimmerman's three SRL phases.
> **Back**: **Forethought**: *Direction* (goal specifies which activities warrant attention and effort); *Strategy activation* (specific goal triggers planning of the relevant strategies); *Persistence-scaffolding* (commitment formation crosses the Rubicon, establishing the volitional foundation for sustained effort). **Performance**: *Effort* mobilization (discrepancy-monitoring drives energy expenditure proportional to gap and goal commitment); *Persistence* (action orientation and volitional control mechanisms sustain effort despite difficulty). **Self-Reflection**: *Strategy activation continued* (failure attribution that targets strategy rather than ability triggers adaptive strategy search for the next cycle).

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[goal-setting-and-self-regulated-learning-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Q:** Definition | Self-Regulated Learning
> **A:** **Front**: Define self-regulated learning (SRL) in terms of what it requires across cognitive, volitional, and motivational dimensions.
> **Back**: **Self-Regulated Learning**: the degree to which learners are metacognitively, motivationally, and behaviorally active participants in their own learning (Zimmerman). **Cognitively**: learners monitor comprehension, plan strategically, and evaluate strategies adaptively. **Volitionally**: learners protect goal pursuit against competing demands, implement intentions systematically, and manage emotional states that would otherwise disrupt engagement. **Motivationally**: learners pursue learning with mastery orientation, autonomous regulation, and high task-specific self-efficacy. SRL is the integrated operation of all three dimensions; impairment in any single dimension degrades the whole system.

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-pkm-foundational-report-2026-04-12]])*
> **Q:** Flashcard 1 — Definition
> **A:** **Q:** How did Flavell (1976) define metacognition, and what are its two major components as distinguished by Brown (1987)?
> **A:** Flavell defined metacognition as "cognition about cognition" — thinking about one's own thinking processes. Brown distinguished two components: *knowledge of cognition* (awareness of cognitive processes, strategies, and states — including declarative, procedural, and conditional knowledge) and *regulation of cognition* (executive control including planning, monitoring, and evaluating).
> **Source:** Section I
> **Difficulty:** Basic
> **Tags:** #metacognition, #definition, #foundational

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-pkm-foundational-report-2026-04-12]])*
> **Q:** Flashcard 2 — Distinction
> **A:** **Q:** What is the difference between a judgment of learning (JOL) and a feeling of knowing (FOK)?
> **A:** JOLs occur *during or after study* and estimate how well material has been encoded ("How well have I learned this?"). FOKs occur *during failed retrieval* and estimate the likelihood of future recognition ("I can't recall this now, but I think I would recognise it"). JOLs assess encoding quality; FOKs assess the residual trace of information that cannot be currently retrieved.
> **Source:** Section III
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #metacognitive-monitoring, #distinction

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-pkm-foundational-report-2026-04-12]])*
> **Q:** Flashcard 3 — Process
> **A:** **Q:** Describe the three phases of Zimmerman's self-regulated learning cycle and their PKM workflow equivalents.
> **A:** (1) *Forethought phase* (goal-setting, strategic planning) → PKM capture and planning workflows. (2) *Performance phase* (strategy implementation, self-monitoring) → Active note-making with elaboration and connection. (3) *Self-reflection phase* (self-judgment, self-reaction) → Review, evaluation, and system modification.
> **Source:** Section IV
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #self-regulated-learning, #pkm, #process

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-pkm-foundational-report-2026-04-12]])*
> **Q:** Flashcard 4 — Connection
> **A:** **Q:** How does the fluency illusion undermine metacognitive calibration in the context of PKM practice?
> **A:** The fluency illusion causes practitioners to mistake *familiarity with material* for *understanding of material*. In PKM, re-reading one's own notes produces high processing fluency (the text is familiar), which the monitoring system misinterprets as evidence of comprehension. This inflates confidence without improving actual knowledge, worsening calibration. The antidote is retrieval-based review: attempting to recall content before reading it.
> **Source:** Sections III, V
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #fluency-illusion, #calibration, #pkm

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-pkm-foundational-report-2026-04-12]])*
> **Q:** Flashcard 5 — Application
> **A:** **Q:** What are the three tiers of the Extended Metacognitive Architecture Model (EMAM)?
> **A:** *Tier 1: Internal metacognition* — classical neural monitoring and regulation (flexible but noisy). *Tier 2: Scaffolded metacognition* — external systems that support internal processes (templates, visualisations, schedules; reduces bias but requires active engagement). *Tier 3: Extended metacognition* — external systems that *constitute* metacognitive processes through functional integration (algorithms that perform monitoring/control autonomously; most reliable but risks atrophy).
> **Source:** Section VI
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #emam, #extended-metacognition, #framework

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-pkm-foundational-report-2026-04-12]])*
> **Q:** Flashcard 6 — Distinction
> **A:** **Q:** What is the key difference between scaffolded metacognition (Tier 2) and extended metacognition (Tier 3) in the EMAM?
> **A:** In *scaffolded metacognition*, the cognitive agent remains the locus of metacognitive processing — the external system provides input and structure, but the human does the monitoring/regulation work. In *extended metacognition*, the external system *performs* the metacognitive functions autonomously through functional integration — the processing is genuinely distributed between internal and external components. The distinction turns on whether the human or the system is doing the metacognitive work.
> **Source:** Section VI
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #emam, #distinction, #extended-mind

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-pkm-foundational-report-2026-04-12]])*
> **Q:** Flashcard 7 — Connection
> **A:** **Q:** What is the monitoring-control coupling, and why does it matter for PKM design?
> **A:** The monitoring-control coupling (Nelson & Narens) is the degree to which monitoring outputs are effectively translated into regulatory control actions. High coupling: problem detected → corrective action taken. Low coupling: problem detected → no effective response. PKM design can tighten this coupling by embedding regulatory responses in monitoring mechanisms (e.g., spaced repetition adjusting review difficulty automatically) and make it visible through logging both monitoring events and regulatory responses.
> **Source:** Section IV
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #monitoring-control-coupling, #pkm-design

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-pkm-foundational-report-2026-04-12]])*
> **Q:** Flashcard 8 — Process
> **A:** **Q:** List the four phases of the Metacognitive PKM Lifecycle and the dominant metacognitive characteristic of each.
> **A:** (1) *Unconscious Capture* — metacognitive monitoring dominated by fluency illusions; regulation ad hoc. (2) *Structured Processing* — external scaffolding provides regulatory structure; monitoring improves through retrieval practice. (3) *Reflective Integration* — practitioner monitors and regulates *system use* itself; calibration improves. (4) *Metacognitive Mastery* — flexible, context-sensitive regulation; conscious management of the internal-external metacognition balance.
> **Source:** Section VII
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #lifecycle, #development, #pkm

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-pkm-foundational-report-2026-04-12]])*
> **Q:** Flashcard 9 — Definition
> **A:** **Q:** What is cognitive offloading, and what is the "PKM calibration paradox" it creates?
> **A:** Cognitive offloading is using external resources to reduce internal cognitive demands. The PKM calibration paradox: creating comprehensive notes can *worsen* calibration because the practitioner mistakes *access fluency* (knowing where to find information in their system) for *retrieval fluency* (actually knowing the information). The notes serve as external memory that the practitioner mistakenly attributes to their internal memory, inflating confidence.
> **Source:** Section V
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #cognitive-offloading, #calibration, #paradox

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-pkm-foundational-report-2026-04-12]])*
> **Q:** Flashcard 10 — Connection
> **A:** **Q:** How does the parity principle from the extended mind thesis apply to metacognitive tools?
> **A:** The parity principle states: if an external process functions in a way that, were it done internally, we would count it as cognitive, then it IS cognitive regardless of physical location. Applied to metacognition: if a PKM system's spaced repetition algorithm performs the same function as an internal FOK judgment (assessing whether knowledge is sufficiently consolidated for retrieval), the parity principle suggests we should count it as a metacognitive process — making the system part of the agent's metacognitive architecture.
> **Source:** Section VI
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #parity-principle, #extended-mind, #metacognition

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-pkm-pkb-foundational-report-2026-04-12]])*
> **Q:** Flashcard 1 — Definition
> **A:** **Q:** What are the two main components of metacognition according to the distinction introduced by Ann Brown?
> **A:** Knowledge-of-cognition (declarative awareness of one's own cognitive processes, abilities, and strategies) and regulation-of-cognition (the active management of cognitive processes through planning, monitoring, and evaluating).
> **Source:** Section 1.2
> **Difficulty:** Basic
> **Tags:** #metacognition, #ann-brown, #foundational-concepts

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-pkm-pkb-foundational-report-2026-04-12]])*
> **Q:** Flashcard 2 — Distinction
> **A:** **Q:** What is the difference between cognitive offloading and metacognitive externalization?
> **A:** Cognitive offloading replaces internal cognitive work with external support (e.g., a calculator replacing mental arithmetic). Metacognitive externalization extends and amplifies internal metacognitive work by rendering it in persistent, inspectable form (e.g., a PKB making knowledge-state assessments visible and reviewable). The key distinction: offloading substitutes; externalization scaffolds.
> **Source:** Section 3.1
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #metacognitive-externalization, #cognitive-offloading, #key-distinction

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-pkm-pkb-foundational-report-2026-04-12]])*
> **Q:** Flashcard 3 — Process
> **A:** **Q:** Name the four types of metacognitive monitoring judgments in the Nelson-Narens taxonomy, in their typical temporal order relative to learning.
> **A:** (1) Ease-of-learning judgments (before study), (2) Judgments of learning (during or after study), (3) Feeling of knowing (during retrieval attempts), (4) Retrospective confidence judgments (after retrieval).
> **Source:** Section 1.4
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #nelson-narens, #metacognitive-monitoring, #metacognitive-judgments

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-pkm-pkb-foundational-report-2026-04-12]])*
> **Q:** Flashcard 4 — Application
> **A:** **Q:** How does note quality function as an externalized "frozen JOL"?
> **A:** A note's elaboration depth, quality of paraphrasing, presence of original examples, and density of connections serve as persistent evidence of the writer's learning depth at creation time. Unlike an internal JOL (which fades in seconds), the note preserves this assessment for future review, enabling more accurate retrospective evaluation of learning.
> **Source:** Section 3.2
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #judgment-of-learning, #pkb-practice, #monitoring

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-pkm-pkb-foundational-report-2026-04-12]])*
> **Q:** Flashcard 5 — Connection
> **A:** **Q:** What are the three levels of the Metacognitive Externalization Spectrum?
> **A:** Level 1 (Implicit) — PKB passively accumulates metacognitive traces; Level 2 (Structural) — PKB architecture deliberately embodies metacognitive knowledge via templates and note types; Level 3 (Reflective) — practitioner maintains an explicit metacognitive layer including calibration logs, strategy experiments, and metacognitive reviews.
> **Source:** Section 4.4
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #metacognitive-externalization-spectrum, #original-contribution, #pkb-design

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-pkm-pkb-foundational-report-2026-04-12]])*
> **Q:** Flashcard 6 — Definition
> **A:** **Q:** What is the PKB Fluency Trap?
> **A:** The paradox in which a well-organized, accessible PKB undermines metacognitive accuracy because organizational quality generates processing fluency, which is misinterpreted as genuine understanding, reducing the practitioner's motivation for effortful processing and producing a gap between apparent and actual knowledge.
> **Source:** Section 6.1
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #fluency-trap, #calibration-paradox, #metacognitive-bias

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-pkm-pkb-foundational-report-2026-04-12]])*
> **Q:** Flashcard 7 — Connection
> **A:** **Q:** What are the three dimensions of the Metacognitive Scaffolding Design Triangle?
> **A:** (1) Monitoring Fidelity — system generates accurate, diagnostic signals about knowledge state; (2) Control Precision — system supports precise, adaptive regulatory interventions; (3) Reflective Integration — system supports metacognitive scrutiny of its own use. Effective design addresses all three; neglecting any one reduces the system's metacognitive value.
> **Source:** Section 7.2
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #design-triangle, #original-contribution, #pkb-design

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-pkm-pkb-foundational-report-2026-04-12]])*
> **Q:** Flashcard 8 — Distinction
> **A:** **Q:** What is pseudometacognition in the context of PKB practice?
> **A:** The condition where the external apparatus of metacognitive regulation (dashboards, analytics, gap detectors) is present without corresponding internal regulatory activity. The practitioner observes monitoring data without engaging in the regulatory reasoning that monitoring should inform — the appearance of metacognitive engagement without the substance.
> **Source:** Section 3.3, A.1
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #pseudometacognition, #monitoring-control-decoupling, #failure-mode

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-pkm-pkb-foundational-report-2026-04-12]])*
> **Q:** Flashcard 9 — Process
> **A:** **Q:** What four transformations does PKB practice apply to metacognitive experiences?
> **A:** (1) Fleeting → Durable — transient metacognitive states become persistent records; (2) Private → Inspectable — subjective states become visible evidence; (3) Unidimensional → Layered — holistic impressions decompose into multi-component assessments; (4) Affect-driven → Evidence-driven — feelings of knowing give way to verifiable knowledge evaluation.
> **Source:** Section 5.2
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #metacognitive-experiences, #pkb-practice, #transformation

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 1 — Definition
> **A:** **Q:** What is comprehension monitoring, and at what levels does it operate?
> **A:** The continuous metacognitive evaluation of text representation adequacy against multiple standards (lexical, propositional, coherence, situation-model). Failures at any level constitute candidate triggers for regulatory response. Most poor comprehenders monitor at lexical/surface levels but neglect coherence and situation-model levels.
> **Source:** Phase II, Section 2.1; Phase IV, Section 4.1
> **Difficulty:** Basic
> **Tags:** #metacognition, #reading, #comprehension-monitoring

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 2 — Distinction
> **A:** **Q:** What is the difference between the textbase and the situation model, and why does the distinction matter for reading comprehension?
> **A:** The textbase is a propositional representation of what the text explicitly states; the situation model is the reader's integrated mental representation of the state of affairs described, enriched by inference and prior knowledge. Only situation-model construction constitutes deep comprehension; textbase representation supports only surface paraphrasing.
> **Source:** Phase II, Section 2.2
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #reading, #situation-model, #textbase

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 3 — Definition
> **A:** **Q:** What is the fluency illusion and what cognitive mechanism produces it?
> **A:** The misattribution of surface-reading fluency (decoding ease, lexical retrieval speed) to comprehension depth. Produced by the monitoring system's reliance on processing ease as a comprehension signal — but fluency carries information about surface-level processing, not situation-model construction. Cause: monitoring operates at the wrong level of text representation.
> **Source:** Phase II, Section 2.2
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #metacognition, #fluency-illusion, #monitoring-failure

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 4 — Process
> **A:** **Q:** Describe the Nelson-Narens monitoring-control architecture as applied to reading.
> **A:** Object level = direct text processing (decoding, parsing, semantic integration). Meta level = metacognitive monitoring of object-level processes. Monitoring flows upward: represents state of comprehension. Control flows downward: adjusts object-level strategy in response. Effective comprehension monitoring requires: (1) accurate monitoring signals, (2) reliable monitoring-control coupling, (3) appropriate control responses.
> **Source:** Phase II, Section 2.3
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #nelson-narens, #metacognitive-monitoring, #reading

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 5 — Distinction
> **A:** **Q:** What is the difference between metacognitive monitoring failure and motivational disengagement in the context of reading comprehension deficits?
> **A:** Monitoring failure = the reader genuinely does not detect comprehension breakdown (cognitive deficit in the detection mechanism). Motivational disengagement = the reader detects failure but suppresses regulatory response (motivationally driven suppression, often to protect self-efficacy). These two pathways require different instructional responses.
> **Source:** Phase VII, Section 3 (Tensions)
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #metacognition, #motivation, #comprehension-monitoring

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 6 — Definition
> **A:** **Q:** What are declarative, procedural, and conditional metacognitive knowledge, and how do they apply to reading strategy instruction?
> **A:** Declarative = knowing *that* (strategy names, self-knowledge); Procedural = knowing *how* (strategy execution); Conditional = knowing *when and why* (appropriateness conditions). Reading strategy instruction most commonly develops only declarative and procedural knowledge; conditional knowledge — the most critical for transfer — is most commonly neglected.
> **Source:** Phase III, Section 3.3
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #metacognitive-knowledge, #strategy-instruction, #reading

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 7 — Application
> **A:** **Q:** What are the four strategies in reciprocal teaching and what metacognitive function does each perform?
> **A:** (1) Predicting — activates prior knowledge, establishes comprehension goals; (2) Questioning — enforces self-monitoring via explicit comprehension question generation; (3) Clarifying — comprehension monitoring and fix-up strategy deployment for detected failures; (4) Summarizing — coherence evaluation at the discourse level, tests situation model construction.
> **Source:** Phase V, Section 5.1
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #reciprocal-teaching, #metacognitive-strategies, #reading

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 8 — Connection
> **A:** **Q:** How does Verbose Efficiency Theory connect decoding fluency to reading comprehension via the working memory mechanism?
> **A:** Inefficient decoding (non-automatic lexical access) consumes working memory resources with lexical-phonological retrieval, leaving insufficient capacity for comprehension processes (coherence monitoring, inference generation, situation-model construction). Therefore, reading fluency is a necessary (though not sufficient) condition for metacognitive comprehension monitoring in demanding texts.
> **Source:** Phase IV, Section 4.5
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #verbal-efficiency-theory, #working-memory, #reading-fluency

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 9 — Distinction
> **A:** **Q:** What distinguishes effective annotation strategies from passive highlighting in terms of metacognitive engagement?
> **A:** Passive highlighting = topographic marking of verbatim text; associated with fluency illusion rather than comprehension monitoring. Effective annotation = content-transforming marks (questions, summaries, connections, evaluations) that require comprehension evaluation, inference generation, and prior-knowledge integration. Effective annotation externalizes the metacognitive regulatory dialogue; passive highlighting does not.
> **Source:** Phase V, Section 5.4
> **Difficulty:** Basic
> **Tags:** #annotation, #metacognition, #reading-strategies

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 10 — Process
> **A:** **Q:** What are the four stages of effective fix-up strategy deployment during reading?
> **A:** (1) Signal detection — monitoring detects comprehension failure; (2) Failure diagnosis — reader identifies the level/type of failure (lexical, propositional, coherence, situation-model); (3) Strategy selection — conditional metacognitive knowledge guides response selection; (4) Strategy execution and evaluation — strategy deployed and monitoring re-evaluates whether failure is resolved.
> **Source:** Phase IV, Section 4.2
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #fix-up-strategy, #comprehension-monitoring, #metacognition

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 11 — Connection
> **A:** **Q:** How does the Matthew Effect in reading relate to metacognitive monitoring capacity?
> **A:** Poor readers have reduced metacognitive monitoring capacity because demanding decoding exhausts working memory; reduced monitoring leads to reduced comprehension; reduced comprehension means less schema building and vocabulary growth, which keeps decoding demanding and keeps monitoring capacity suppressed. The failure cycle is: poor decoding → high cognitive load → suppressed monitoring → comprehension failure → reduced vocabulary and schema growth → continued poor decoding.
> **Source:** Phase IV, Section 4.5
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #matthew-effect, #metacognition, #reading, #cognitive-load

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 12 — Definition
> **A:** **Q:** What does "self-regulated reading" mean and how does it relate to Zimmerman's cyclical SRL model?
> **A:** Self-regulated reading is metacognitive, goal-directed, and strategically enacted text comprehension. Maps onto Zimmerman's three phases: (1) Forethought = goal-setting, prior knowledge activation, strategy planning; (2) Performance = comprehension monitoring, strategy deployment, attention regulation; (3) Self-reflection = outcome evaluation, attribution, strategy adaptation. Distinguishes reading as self-directed enterprise from externally regulated strategy use.
> **Source:** Phase III, Section 3.4; Phase II, Section 2.1
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #self-regulated-learning, #reading, #metacognition

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 13 — Application
> **A:** **Q:** What is the KWL strategy, and which metacognitive reading functions does each component serve?
> **A:** K (What do I *Know*?) = prior knowledge activation and establishing comprehension baseline; W (What do I *Want* to know?) = goal-setting and directing monitoring attention; L (What have I *Learned*?) = comprehension evaluation, gap detection, and situation model assessment. Collectively: the KWL sequence operationalizes the forethought-monitoring-self-reflection SRL cycle for a single reading session.
> **Source:** Phase V, Section 5.3
> **Difficulty:** Basic
> **Tags:** #KWL-strategy, #metacognition, #reading

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 14 — Connection
> **A:** **Q:** How does the elaborative interrogation strategy operationalize the depth-of-processing principle in reading?
> **A:** Depth-of-processing principle: semantic/elaborative processing produces more durable encoding than surface processing. Elaborative interrogation operationalizes deep processing by requiring the reader to generate *why/how* explanations for text propositions, thereby enforcing semantic elaboration and prior-knowledge integration. The strategy converts passive proposition reception into active inferential construction — the functional equivalent of forced deep processing.
> **Source:** Phase III, Section 3.5; Phase VII, Lexicon
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #elaborative-interrogation, #levels-of-processing, #reading

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 1 — Definition
> **A:** **Q:** What are the two primary functional components of metacognition according to Schraw and Dennison (1994)?
> **A:** Knowledge of Cognition (what one knows about cognitive processes, tasks, and strategies) and Regulation of Cognition (how one monitors, plans, evaluates, and adjusts ongoing cognitive engagement).
> **Source:** Phase II, Conceptual Foundations
> **Difficulty:** Basic
> **Tags:** #metacognition, #knowledge-of-cognition, #regulation-of-cognition, #schraw

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 2 — Distinction
> **A:** **Q:** How does the Nelson-Narens framework distinguish monitoring from control?
> **A:** Monitoring is the causal relationship flowing from the object-level to the meta-level (information about ongoing cognitive processing flows upward). Control is the reverse: the meta-level issues commands that modify object-level processing. They are analytically distinct but empirically interleaved.
> **Source:** Phase II; Phase IV
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #metacognition, #monitoring, #control, #nelson-narens

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 3 — Distinction
> **A:** **Q:** What distinguishes a Judgment of Learning (JOL) from a Feeling of Knowing (FOK)?
> **A:** A JOL is made after studying an item, estimating future recall probability. A FOK arises specifically after a retrieval failure, estimating whether the unrecalled item could be recognized or retrieved later. JOLs are post-study prospective; FOKs are post-retrieval-failure prospective.
> **Source:** Phase II; Appendix Section 1
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #metacognition, #judgment-of-learning, #feeling-of-knowing, #monitoring

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 4 — Process
> **A:** **Q:** What is the Fluency Illusion and why does it impair metacognitive monitoring accuracy?
> **A:** The Fluency Illusion is the misattribution of processing fluency (ease of processing) as evidence of deep learning or comprehension. It impairs monitoring accuracy because fluency is a non-diagnostic cue for long-term retention — re-reading produces fluency without improving retention, but the learner's JOLs become inflated because the monitoring system uses fluency as its primary cue.
> **Source:** Phase IV; Appendix Section 1
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #metacognition, #fluency-illusion, #monitoring, #calibration

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 5 — Definition
> **A:** **Q:** What is calibration in the metacognitive sense, and what is the predominant direction of miscalibration in the research literature?
> **A:** Calibration is the alignment between subjective confidence and objective accuracy — a well-calibrated learner who expresses 70% confidence should achieve approximately 70% accuracy. The predominant direction of miscalibration is over-confidence: most learners, in most domains, express confidence that exceeds their actual accuracy.
> **Source:** Phase IV
> **Difficulty:** Basic
> **Tags:** #metacognition, #calibration, #overconfidence, #monitoring-accuracy

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 6 — Process
> **A:** **Q:** What is the delayed JOL effect, and what is the theoretical explanation?
> **A:** Delayed JOLs (made 1-2 minutes after study) are substantially more accurate predictors of subsequent recall than immediate JOLs. The explanation is cue-based: delayed JOLs allow time for an accessibility test (partial retrieval attempt), making retrieval fluency the primary cue — which is more diagnostic than the processing fluency cues available immediately after study.
> **Source:** Phase IV
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #metacognition, #judgment-of-learning, #delayed-jol, #cue-utilization

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 7 — Definition
> **A:** **Q:** What is Flavell's distinction between metacognitive knowledge and metacognitive experiences?
> **A:** Metacognitive knowledge is stable, explicitly accessible propositional knowledge about cognitive processes, tasks, and strategies. Metacognitive experiences are phenomenological states that arise during cognitive engagement and carry monitoring information — feelings of difficulty, confidence, familiarity, and satisfaction that signal the quality of ongoing processing in real time.
> **Source:** Phase II
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #metacognition, #flavell, #metacognitive-experience, #metacognitive-knowledge

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 8 — Application
> **A:** **Q:** What is Reciprocal Teaching, and why is it considered the most empirically validated metacognitive instruction method?
> **A:** Reciprocal Teaching (Palincsar & Brown, 1984) uses dialogue-based practice in four comprehension-monitoring strategies (prediction, questioning, clarification, summarization) within a ZPD framework, with a teacher gradually transferring metacognitive responsibility to students. Effect sizes consistently range from 0.4 to 0.9 on reading comprehension measures. It is most validated because it addresses both monitoring (comprehension standards) and regulation (strategy deployment) while using the Vygotskian scaffolding mechanism.
> **Source:** Phase V
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #metacognition, #reciprocal-teaching, #comprehension-monitoring, #instruction

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 9 — Distinction
> **A:** **Q:** Distinguish declarative, procedural, and conditional metacognitive knowledge.
> **A:** Declarative: propositional knowledge about cognitive processes and one's own cognitive characteristics (knowing that distributed practice outperforms massed practice). Procedural: knowledge of how to execute cognitive strategies (knowing how to implement retrieval practice). Conditional: knowledge of when and why to deploy particular strategies — the discriminative competence specifying appropriate context for each strategy. Conditional knowledge is the most neglected and most practically significant.
> **Source:** Phase II
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #metacognition, #conditional-knowledge, #metacognitive-knowledge

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 10 — Connection
> **A:** **Q:** How does the Dunning-Kruger effect relate to Nelson-Narens' monitoring-control architecture?
> **A:** The Dunning-Kruger effect — low-competence individuals' greater over-confidence — is a direct instantiation of monitoring failure in the Nelson-Narens framework. Low domain knowledge impairs both object-level performance and meta-level monitoring accuracy (because the knowledge required to detect performance failures is the same domain knowledge lacking in poor performers). The meta-level's model of object-level performance is thus doubly impaired.
> **Source:** Phase IV
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #metacognition, #dunning-kruger, #calibration, #nelson-narens

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 11 — Application
> **A:** **Q:** What is the calibration-regulation gap, and what variables are known to close it?
> **A:** The calibration-regulation gap is the discrepancy between accurate monitoring (detecting comprehension failures or performance gaps) and effective regulatory action (initiating corrective strategies). Accurate detection does not guarantee correction. Variables known to close the gap include: growth mindset orientation (interpreting difficulty as actionable information), mastery goal orientation (focusing on improvement rather than performance demonstration), and high self-efficacy for regulatory action.
> **Source:** Phase IV; Phase V
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #metacognition, #calibration, #regulation, #growth-mindset

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 12 — Definition
> **A:** **Q:** What is pseudometacognition, and what practical risk does it pose?
> **A:** Pseudometacognition is the performance of external metacognitive behavior patterns (completing monitoring checklists, articulating study plans, answering self-questioning prompts) without genuine internal monitoring or regulatory adjustment. The practical risk is that learners taught explicit metacognitive protocols may comply with the external script without developing genuine regulatory competence — the protocol becomes a performance rather than a cognitive tool.
> **Source:** Phase V; Appendix Section 1
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #metacognition, #pseudometacognition, #metacognitive-instruction

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 13 — Process
> **A:** **Q:** Why does comprehension monitoring fail in novice/immature readers, according to Brown's research?
> **A:** Novice readers typically monitor only against the lexical standard (do I know the words?), missing higher-order cohesion and consistency standards. This produces the paradox of feeling comprehension has occurred (because words were decoded) when in fact no coherent situation model has been constructed. Skill development involves expanding the standards against which monitoring operates, not merely the monitoring process itself.
> **Source:** Phase IV
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #metacognition, #comprehension-monitoring, #brown, #situation-models

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 14 — Distinction
> **A:** **Q:** What does the Nelson-Narens framework mean by the "monitoring-first principle"?
> **A:** The monitoring-first principle is the theoretical claim that regulation can be no more accurate than the monitoring on which it is based: accurate monitoring is a necessary precondition for appropriate regulatory action. If monitoring is inaccurate (inflated confidence from fluency-based cues), even sophisticated regulatory strategies will be deployed at the wrong times or not deployed when needed. The practical implication is that metacognitive instruction must target monitoring accuracy, not merely regulatory strategy knowledge.
> **Source:** Phase IV
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #metacognition, #monitoring, #control, #nelson-narens, #calibration

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 15 — Connection
> **A:** **Q:** How does the Extended Mind Theory ground the claim that PKB architecture can function as external metacognitive infrastructure?
> **A:** The Extended Mind Theory (Clark & Chalmers) holds that cognitive processes can be genuinely extended into the environment through well-designed cognitive scaffolding — tools that satisfy the parity principle (functioning as they would if they occurred internally). A PKB's wiki-link structure externalizes knowledge connection monitoring; SRS scheduling externalizes JOL-based study termination decisions. These are not mere aids to cognition but genuine extensions of metacognitive monitoring and control function.
> **Source:** Phase V; Phase VI
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #metacognition, #extended-mind-theory, #pkb, #metacognitive-infrastructure

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognitive-development-foundational-report-2026-04-09]])*
> **Q:** Metacognition Definition (Basic)
> **A:** **Q:** What is the fundamental distinction captured by the term "metacognition"?
> **A:** Metacognition is cognition about cognition — a meta level that monitors, evaluates, and regulates the operations of an object level (the cognitive processes actually engaged in a task). The key structural feature is the hierarchical separation between the monitoring/regulating level and the processes being monitored/regulated.
> **Source:** Section 1, Section 4
> **Difficulty:** Basic
> **Tags:** #metacognition #definitions

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognitive-development-foundational-report-2026-04-09]])*
> **Q:** Monitoring vs. Control Distinction (Basic)
> **A:** **Q:** What is the functional distinction between metacognitive monitoring and metacognitive control in the Nelson-Narens framework?
> **A:** Monitoring is the flow of information *upward* from the object level to the meta level — assessments of the current state of cognitive operations (JOLs, FOK, comprehension monitoring signals). Control is the flow of information *downward* from the meta level to the object level — decisions that modify, redirect, or terminate cognitive processes (study time allocation, strategy selection, help-seeking). The two can fail independently.
> **Source:** Section 3, Section 4
> **Difficulty:** Basic
> **Tags:** #metacognitive-monitoring #metacognitive-control

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognitive-development-foundational-report-2026-04-09]])*
> **Q:** Fluency Trap Mechanism (Intermediate)
> **A:** **Q:** What is the fluency trap, and why does it specifically cause calibration failure during re-studying?
> **A:** The fluency trap is the metacognitive monitoring error arising from treating processing fluency (experienced ease of processing) as evidence of deep understanding or durable encoding. Re-studying already-encountered material generates increased fluency through familiarity, not through genuine re-encoding of conceptual structure. The monitoring system interprets this familiarity-based fluency as evidence of superior learning, producing elevated JOLs and overconfidence in comprehension quality.
> **Source:** Section 3, Section 7
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #fluency-trap #calibration #monitoring-accuracy

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognitive-development-foundational-report-2026-04-09]])*
> **Q:** Co-Developmental Constraint (Intermediate)
> **A:** **Q:** What is the co-developmental constraint, and what does it imply about domain-general metacognitive skills training?
> **A:** The co-developmental constraint is the structural limit whereby domain-specific monitoring accuracy cannot substantially surpass domain competence, because accurate performance monitoring requires a representation of excellent performance that only develops through substantial domain experience. Implication: generic metacognitive skills training divorced from domain content will produce limited calibration accuracy transfer, because the monitoring schemas needed for domain-specific accuracy are domain-bound.
> **Source:** Section 3
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #co-developmental-constraint #domain-specific #calibration

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognitive-development-foundational-report-2026-04-09]])*
> **Q:** Delayed JOL Advantage (Intermediate)
> **A:** **Q:** Why are delayed JOLs more accurate predictors of future test performance than immediate JOLs?
> **A:** Immediate JOLs are heavily influenced by study-time fluency — the ease of the just-completed study episode — which is only weakly predictive of future recall. Delayed JOLs (made 24 hours after study) require actual retrieval from memory at the time of judgment, making them functionally similar to a test. Retrieval-based monitoring signals are considerably more accurate predictors of future test performance than fluency-based monitoring signals.
> **Source:** Section 3
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #judgment-of-learning #delayed-jol #calibration

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognitive-development-foundational-report-2026-04-09]])*
> **Q:** Monitoring-Control Decoupling (Advanced)
> **A:** **Q:** What are the three characteristic decoupling failure modes in the monitoring-control coupling, and what distinguishes them?
> **A:** (1) Detection-correction gap: Monitoring detects a problem but no corrective control response is initiated — the learner senses confusion but continues passively. (2) Control-without-monitoring: Control responses (strategy switching) are initiated without basis in accurate monitoring signals — decisions based on subjective preference rather than genuine performance assessment. (3) Automaticity-induced monitoring suppression: Highly automated procedures operate below the monitoring threshold, so errors in automated routines are not detected by the monitoring system.
> **Source:** Section 4
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #monitoring-control-coupling #metacognitive-regulation

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognitive-development-foundational-report-2026-04-09]])*
> **Q:** Standards Inadequacy as Monitoring Failure Source (Advanced)
> **A:** **Q:** Winne and Hadwin's COPES model identifies standards inadequacy as a monitoring failure source distinct from cue-utilization error. Explain the distinction.
> **A:** Cue-utilization error: The monitoring system is functional and uses available cues, but uses the wrong cues (cues with low validity for the performance dimension being assessed). Standards inadequacy: The monitoring system cannot generate accurate assessments because the learner lacks sufficiently specified criteria for what excellent performance looks like — the reference standard for comparison is absent or impoverished. Interventions differ: cue-utilization errors require accuracy feedback; standards inadequacy requires standards enrichment (deep study of exemplary work).
> **Source:** Section 6
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #standards-inadequacy #monitoring-failure #metacognitive-knowledge

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognitive-development-foundational-report-2026-04-09]])*
> **Q:** Reciprocal Teaching Components (Basic)
> **A:** **Q:** What are the four metacognitive strategies specifically targeted in reciprocal teaching?
> **A:** Summarizing (identifying main ideas and constructing a working model), questioning (generating inferential and evaluative questions requiring interpretation), clarifying (identifying comprehension failures and pursuing resolution), and predicting (anticipating the text's direction based on structure and content clues).
> **Source:** Section 8
> **Difficulty:** Basic
> **Tags:** #reciprocal-teaching #metacognitive-instruction #comprehension-monitoring

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognitive-development-foundational-report-2026-04-09]])*
> **Q:** Recursive Self-Governance Concept (Advanced)
> **A:** **Q:** What is recursive self-governance, and why is it presented as a more complete frame for metacognitive development than monitoring-control improvement alone?
> **A:** Recursive self-governance is the capacity of a cognitive system to monitor, evaluate, and modify not merely its object-level performance but its own performance-monitoring-and-modification processes. It is more complete because it captures the developmental continuity across expertise levels: each meaningful advance in domain competence requires recalibration of the monitoring apparatus — a higher-order metacognitive operation — and lifelong metacognitive development involves repeated rebuilding of the monitoring system at increasingly sophisticated levels, not merely one-time calibration improvement.
> **Source:** Synthesis section
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #recursive-self-governance #metacognitive-development

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognitive-development-foundational-report-2026-04-09]])*
> **Q:** Developmental Trajectory: Metacognitive Agency (Intermediate)
> **A:** **Q:** What is metacognitive agency, and at what developmental period does it typically emerge?
> **A:** Metacognitive agency is the capacity to reflect on one's own learning strategies as objects of inquiry, form goals for improving them, and deliberately restructure learning approaches based on performance feedback — a second-order metacognitive capacity involving monitoring-and-control of the learning system over time. It typically consolidates during adolescence (approximately ages 14–22) concurrent with prefrontal cortical development, and is the metacognitive precondition for genuinely autonomous self-directed learning.
> **Source:** Section 5
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #metacognitive-agency #developmental-trajectory

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognitive-skills-foundational-report-2026-04-09]])*
> **Q:** SR Seed 1 — Definition: Metacognition
> **A:** **Q:** What is Flavell's definition of metacognition, and what two broad categories does it comprise?
> **A:** Metacognition is cognition about cognition — knowledge and processes that take one's own cognitive states and products as their objects. It comprises (a) metacognitive knowledge (stored declarative knowledge about person, task, and strategy factors affecting cognition) and (b) metacognitive experiences (real-time monitoring signals arising during cognitive engagement).
> **Source:** Section 2; Flavell (1979)
> **Difficulty:** Basic
> **Tags:** definition, metacognition, Flavell

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognitive-skills-foundational-report-2026-04-09]])*
> **Q:** SR Seed 2 — Framework: Nelson-Narens
> **A:** **Q:** Describe the two levels and two information flows in the Nelson-Narens metacognitive monitoring-control framework.
> **A:** Object level: first-order cognitive processes (studying, reasoning, retrieving). Meta level: metacognitive processes that observe and control the object level. Upward flow (monitoring): the meta level receives information about the object level's state (via JOLs, FOK, EOL). Downward flow (control): the meta level sends commands that modify object-level processes (study more, stop, seek help).
> **Source:** Section 3
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** framework, Nelson-Narens, monitoring, control

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognitive-skills-foundational-report-2026-04-09]])*
> **Q:** SR Seed 3 — Distinction: Monitoring vs. Regulation
> **A:** **Q:** How do metacognitive monitoring and regulation differ, and why does the monitoring-control gap matter?
> **A:** Monitoring is the metacognitive assessment of one's current cognitive state (JOL, FOK, comprehension check — generating information). Regulation is the behavioral response to that information (study more, switch strategies, seek help — executing change). The monitoring-control gap describes findings that accurate monitoring does not automatically translate into appropriate regulation — learners may detect a comprehension gap without changing their study approach, because regulation is a separate capacity that can fail independently of monitoring.
> **Source:** Sections 3, 5
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** monitoring, regulation, distinction, monitoring-control gap

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognitive-skills-foundational-report-2026-04-09]])*
> **Q:** SR Seed 4 — Mechanism: Fluency Illusion
> **A:** **Q:** Why does rereading feel more productive than retrieval practice, and why is this feeling misleading?
> **A:** Rereading familiar material is processed fluently (quickly, easily, without retrieval failure), and the monitoring system interprets this processing fluency as evidence of deep comprehension — the fluency illusion. Retrieval practice involves frequent retrieval failure, which the monitoring system correctly interprets as difficulty but incorrectly interprets as ineffective learning. In reality, the storage-retrieval paradox means the effortful encoding of retrieval practice produces more durable memory traces, while the fluent rereading of familiar material produces superficial reactivation without strengthened storage.
> **Source:** Sections 4, 7, 8
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** fluency illusion, desirable difficulties, retrieval practice, mechanism

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognitive-skills-foundational-report-2026-04-09]])*
> **Q:** SR Seed 5 — Process: Zimmerman's SRL Cycle
> **A:** **Q:** Name the three phases of Zimmerman's cyclical SRL model and identify one metacognitive process in each.
> **A:** (1) Forethought: task analysis and strategic planning before task engagement — selecting an evidence-based study strategy based on task demands and goals. (2) Performance: self-monitoring and self-instruction during task engagement — detecting comprehension failures and adjusting reading strategy in response.
